case_info.scenario: A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

case_info.explanation: C. Adult polyglucosan body disease The presentation was suggestive of adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD), and a multigene panel revealed a compound heterozygous pathogenic missense variant in the glycogen branching enzyme 1 (GBE1) gene (c.986A>C (p.Tyr329Ser) and c.691 + 2T>C (IVS5 + 2T>C)), confirming this diagnosis.1The Tyr329Ser variant is common in Ashkenazi Jewish patients. APBD is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, in the spectrum of glycogen storage disease type IV, caused by biallelic pathogenicGBE1variants.1-4The clinical presentation is heterogeneous, but the core symptoms include progressive neurogenic bladder, gait dysfunction due to mixed upper and lower motor neuron involvement (ie, myeloneuropathy), and cognitive impairment at or after age 40 years.1-4Lower motor neuron involvement is due to a length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy and polyradiculopathies.1-4In severe cases, an Alzheimer disease–like dementia phenotype was previously reported.1-4The pace of progression is usually slow. In one of the largest series to date, the median age for onset of symptoms was 51 years and for wheelchair dependence and death was 63 and 70 years, respectively.4Radiographic findings may be nonspecific and include widespread confluent and symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter abnormalities in the periventricular regions, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and external capsule. Additional clues that (if present) suggest APBD include involvement of corticospinal tracts and medial lemniscus of the pons and medulla, superior cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei, and medullary and spinal cord atrophy.1-4Although nerve biopsy may show polyglucosan bodies, definitive diagnosis is established by genetic testing via targetedGBE1sequencing, multigene panels that includeGBE1, whole-exome sequencing or whole-genome sequencing.2,3Treatment is supportive and includes symptomatic management of spasticity, neurogenic bladder, dysautonomia, and cognitive decline.2,3 Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation is caused by autosomal recessive variants in theDARS2gene.5Typical presentation occurs in early childhood, but adult-onset disease has been described.5Core clinical features include slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-extremity predominant spasticity, and dorsal column dysfunction.5Axonal neuropathy can occur. MRI reveals a distinct T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the cerebral white matter sparing the U-fibers, involvement of posterior limbs of the internal capsule, splenium of the corpus callosum, trigeminal nerve tracts, cerebellum, and the dorsal column and lateral corticospinal tracts of the medulla and spinal cord.5Features that allow distinction from APBD are an earlier age of onset, prominent cerebellar and sensory ataxia, and characteristic spinal cord signal abnormalities.5 LMNB-1–related autosomal dominant leukodystrophy (ADLD) presents between ages 40 to 60 years with dysautonomia followed by corticospinal tract and cerebellar dysfunction, resulting in spastic ataxia and tremors.6MRI in ADLD can show T2/FLAIR hyperintensity predominantly in a frontoparietal distribution following the corticospinal tracts through the posterior limb of the internal capsule toward the medulla and upper and middle cerebellar peduncles.6,7Spinal cord atrophy is common and can be associated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the entire cord white matter.6,7Some distinguishing features from APBD are the different imaging pattern, sparing of the peripheral nervous system, and more prominent cerebellar dysfunction.6 Alexander disease is caused by autosomal dominantGFAPgene variants that can present across the lifespan, with adult onset occurring in approximately 33% of cases.8The typical adult phenotype includes bulbar symptoms (eg, palatal myoclonus, dysarthria, dysphagia), cerebellar dysfunction, and corticospinal tract involvement resulting in spastic weakness.8,9Other features include sleep disorder, dysautonomia, and parkinsonism.8A typical MRI finding is cervicomedullary atrophy with relative pontine sparing, known as thetadpole sign.8,9Other potential findings include cerebellar signal abnormalities, contrast-enhancing lesions, and periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities.8,9Distinguishing features from APBD include sparing of the peripheral nervous system and lack of the extensive supratentorial signal abnormalities and extensive spinal cord atrophy seen in this case.8,9

dialogue_history.text: Adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD) is a plausible consideration given the Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, progressive upper motor neuron signs, and white matter changes. However, the combination of upper and lower motor neuron involvement, pseudobulbar affect, and sensory axonal neuropathy is highly suggestive of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with frontotemporal dementia (ALS-FTD) spectrum, which also fits the clinical and MRI findings. A focused genetic evaluation for ALS-FTD genes, such as C9orf72, should be prioritized alongside considering APBD.

imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]

[Confidence]

[Cognitive Burden]

  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:

  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,

  }
}

His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). case_info.explanation: C. Adult polyglucosan body disease The presentation was suggestive of adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD), and a multigene panel revealed a compound heterozygous pathogenic missense variant in the glycogen branching enzyme 1 (GBE1) gene (c.986A>C (p.Tyr329Ser) and c.691 + 2T>C (IVS5 + 2T>C)), confirming this diagnosis.1The Tyr329Ser variant is common in Ashkenazi Jewish patients. APBD is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, in the spectrum of glycogen storage disease type IV, caused by biallelic pathogenicGBE1variants.1-4The clinical presentation is heterogeneous, but the core symptoms include progressive neurogenic bladder, gait dysfunction due to mixed upper and lower motor neuron involvement (ie, myeloneuropathy), and cognitive impairment at or after age 40 years.1-4Lower motor neuron involvement is due to a length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy and polyradiculopathies.1-4In severe cases, an Alzheimer disease–like dementia phenotype was previously reported.1-4The pace of progression is usually slow. In one of the largest series to date, the median age for onset of symptoms was 51 years and for wheelchair dependence and death was 63 and 70 years, respectively.4Radiographic findings may be nonspecific and include widespread confluent and symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter abnormalities in the periventricular regions, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and external capsule. Additional clues that (if present) suggest APBD include involvement of corticospinal tracts and medial lemniscus of the pons and medulla, superior cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei, and medullary and spinal cord atrophy.1-4Although nerve biopsy may show polyglucosan bodies, definitive diagnosis is established by genetic testing via targetedGBE1sequencing, multigene panels that includeGBE1, whole-exome sequencing or whole-genome sequencing.2,3Treatment is supportive and includes symptomatic management of spasticity, neurogenic bladder, dysautonomia, and cognitive decline.2,3 Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation is caused by autosomal recessive variants in theDARS2gene.5Typical presentation occurs in early childhood, but adult-onset disease has been described.5Core clinical features include slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-extremity predominant spasticity, and dorsal column dysfunction.5Axonal neuropathy can occur. MRI reveals a distinct T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the cerebral white matter sparing the U-fibers, involvement of posterior limbs of the internal capsule, splenium of the corpus callosum, trigeminal nerve tracts, cerebellum, and the dorsal column and lateral corticospinal tracts of the medulla and spinal cord.5Features that allow distinction from APBD are an earlier age of onset, prominent cerebellar and sensory ataxia, and characteristic spinal cord signal abnormalities.5 LMNB-1–related autosomal dominant leukodystrophy (ADLD) presents between ages 40 to 60 years with dysautonomia followed by corticospinal tract and cerebellar dysfunction, resulting in spastic ataxia and tremors.6MRI in ADLD can show T2/FLAIR hyperintensity predominantly in a frontoparietal distribution following the corticospinal tracts through the posterior limb of the internal capsule toward the medulla and upper and middle cerebellar peduncles.6,7Spinal cord atrophy is common and can be associated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the entire cord white matter.6,7Some distinguishing features from APBD are the different imaging pattern, sparing of the peripheral nervous system, and more prominent cerebellar dysfunction.6 Alexander disease is caused by autosomal dominantGFAPgene variants that can present across the lifespan, with adult onset occurring in approximately 33% of cases.8The typical adult phenotype includes bulbar symptoms (eg, palatal myoclonus, dysarthria, dysphagia), cerebellar dysfunction, and corticospinal tract involvement resulting in spastic weakness.8,9Other features include sleep disorder, dysautonomia, and parkinsonism.8A typical MRI finding is cervicomedullary atrophy with relative pontine sparing, known as thetadpole sign.8,9Other potential findings include cerebellar signal abnormalities, contrast-enhancing lesions, and periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities.8,9Distinguishing features from APBD include sparing of the peripheral nervous system and lack of the extensive supratentorial signal abnormalities and extensive spinal cord atrophy seen in this case.8,9

A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. case_info.explanation: C. Adult polyglucosan body disease The presentation was suggestive of adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD), and a multigene panel revealed a compound heterozygous pathogenic missense variant in the glycogen branching enzyme 1 (GBE1) gene (c.986A>C (p.Tyr329Ser) and c.691 + 2T>C (IVS5 + 2T>C)), confirming this diagnosis.1The Tyr329Ser variant is common in Ashkenazi Jewish patients. APBD is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, in the spectrum of glycogen storage disease type IV, caused by biallelic pathogenicGBE1variants.1-4The clinical presentation is heterogeneous, but the core symptoms include progressive neurogenic bladder, gait dysfunction due to mixed upper and lower motor neuron involvement (ie, myeloneuropathy), and cognitive impairment at or after age 40 years.1-4Lower motor neuron involvement is due to a length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy and polyradiculopathies.1-4In severe cases, an Alzheimer disease–like dementia phenotype was previously reported.1-4The pace of progression is usually slow. In one of the largest series to date, the median age for onset of symptoms was 51 years and for wheelchair dependence and death was 63 and 70 years, respectively.4Radiographic findings may be nonspecific and include widespread confluent and symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter abnormalities in the periventricular regions, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and external capsule. Additional clues that (if present) suggest APBD include involvement of corticospinal tracts and medial lemniscus of the pons and medulla, superior cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei, and medullary and spinal cord atrophy.1-4Although nerve biopsy may show polyglucosan bodies, definitive diagnosis is established by genetic testing via targetedGBE1sequencing, multigene panels that includeGBE1, whole-exome sequencing or whole-genome sequencing.2,3Treatment is supportive and includes symptomatic management of spasticity, neurogenic bladder, dysautonomia, and cognitive decline.2,3 Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation is caused by autosomal recessive variants in theDARS2gene.5Typical presentation occurs in early childhood, but adult-onset disease has been described.5Core clinical features include slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-extremity predominant spasticity, and dorsal column dysfunction.5Axonal neuropathy can occur. MRI reveals a distinct T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the cerebral white matter sparing the U-fibers, involvement of posterior limbs of the internal capsule, splenium of the corpus callosum, trigeminal nerve tracts, cerebellum, and the dorsal column and lateral corticospinal tracts of the medulla and spinal cord.5Features that allow distinction from APBD are an earlier age of onset, prominent cerebellar and sensory ataxia, and characteristic spinal cord signal abnormalities.5 LMNB-1–related autosomal dominant leukodystrophy (ADLD) presents between ages 40 to 60 years with dysautonomia followed by corticospinal tract and cerebellar dysfunction, resulting in spastic ataxia and tremors.6MRI in ADLD can show T2/FLAIR hyperintensity predominantly in a frontoparietal distribution following the corticospinal tracts through the posterior limb of the internal capsule toward the medulla and upper and middle cerebellar peduncles.6,7Spinal cord atrophy is common and can be associated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the entire cord white matter.6,7Some distinguishing features from APBD are the different imaging pattern, sparing of the peripheral nervous system, and more prominent cerebellar dysfunction.6 Alexander disease is caused by autosomal dominantGFAPgene variants that can present across the lifespan, with adult onset occurring in approximately 33% of cases.8The typical adult phenotype includes bulbar symptoms (eg, palatal myoclonus, dysarthria, dysphagia), cerebellar dysfunction, and corticospinal tract involvement resulting in spastic weakness.8,9Other features include sleep disorder, dysautonomia, and parkinsonism.8A typical MRI finding is cervicomedullary atrophy with relative pontine sparing, known as thetadpole sign.8,9Other potential findings include cerebellar signal abnormalities, contrast-enhancing lesions, and periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities.8,9Distinguishing features from APBD include sparing of the peripheral nervous system and lack of the extensive supratentorial signal abnormalities and extensive spinal cord atrophy seen in this case.8,9

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Adult polyglucosan body disease The presentation was suggestive of adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD), and a multigene panel revealed a compound heterozygous pathogenic missense variant in the glycogen branching enzyme 1 (GBE1) gene (c.986A>C (p.Tyr329Ser) and c.691 + 2T>C (IVS5 + 2T>C)), confirming this diagnosis.1The Tyr329Ser variant is common in Ashkenazi Jewish patients. APBD is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, in the spectrum of glycogen storage disease type IV, caused by biallelic pathogenicGBE1variants.1-4The clinical presentation is heterogeneous, but the core symptoms include progressive neurogenic bladder, gait dysfunction due to mixed upper and lower motor neuron involvement (ie, myeloneuropathy), and cognitive impairment at or after age 40 years.1-4Lower motor neuron involvement is due to a length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy and polyradiculopathies.1-4In severe cases, an Alzheimer disease–like dementia phenotype was previously reported.1-4The pace of progression is usually slow. In one of the largest series to date, the median age for onset of symptoms was 51 years and for wheelchair dependence and death was 63 and 70 years, respectively.4Radiographic findings may be nonspecific and include widespread confluent and symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter abnormalities in the periventricular regions, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and external capsule. Additional clues that (if present) suggest APBD include involvement of corticospinal tracts and medial lemniscus of the pons and medulla, superior cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei, and medullary and spinal cord atrophy.1-4Although nerve biopsy may show polyglucosan bodies, definitive diagnosis is established by genetic testing via targetedGBE1sequencing, multigene panels that includeGBE1, whole-exome sequencing or whole-genome sequencing.2,3Treatment is supportive and includes symptomatic management of spasticity, neurogenic bladder, dysautonomia, and cognitive decline.2,3 Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation is caused by autosomal recessive variants in theDARS2gene.5Typical presentation occurs in early childhood, but adult-onset disease has been described.5Core clinical features include slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-extremity predominant spasticity, and dorsal column dysfunction.5Axonal neuropathy can occur. MRI reveals a distinct T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the cerebral white matter sparing the U-fibers, involvement of posterior limbs of the internal capsule, splenium of the corpus callosum, trigeminal nerve tracts, cerebellum, and the dorsal column and lateral corticospinal tracts of the medulla and spinal cord.5Features that allow distinction from APBD are an earlier age of onset, prominent cerebellar and sensory ataxia, and characteristic spinal cord signal abnormalities.5 LMNB-1–related autosomal dominant leukodystrophy (ADLD) presents between ages 40 to 60 years with dysautonomia followed by corticospinal tract and cerebellar dysfunction, resulting in spastic ataxia and tremors.6MRI in ADLD can show T2/FLAIR hyperintensity predominantly in a frontoparietal distribution following the corticospinal tracts through the posterior limb of the internal capsule toward the medulla and upper and middle cerebellar peduncles.6,7Spinal cord atrophy is common and can be associated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the entire cord white matter.6,7Some distinguishing features from APBD are the different imaging pattern, sparing of the peripheral nervous system, and more prominent cerebellar dysfunction.6 Alexander disease is caused by autosomal dominantGFAPgene variants that can present across the lifespan, with adult onset occurring in approximately 33% of cases.8The typical adult phenotype includes bulbar symptoms (eg, palatal myoclonus, dysarthria, dysphagia), cerebellar dysfunction, and corticospinal tract involvement resulting in spastic weakness.8,9Other features include sleep disorder, dysautonomia, and parkinsonism.8A typical MRI finding is cervicomedullary atrophy with relative pontine sparing, known as thetadpole sign.8,9Other potential findings include cerebellar signal abnormalities, contrast-enhancing lesions, and periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities.8,9Distinguishing features from APBD include sparing of the peripheral nervous system and lack of the extensive supratentorial signal abnormalities and extensive spinal cord atrophy seen in this case.8,9

A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. case_info.explanation: C. Adult polyglucosan body disease The presentation was suggestive of adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD), and a multigene panel revealed a compound heterozygous pathogenic missense variant in the glycogen branching enzyme 1 (GBE1) gene (c.986A>C (p.Tyr329Ser) and c.691 + 2T>C (IVS5 + 2T>C)), confirming this diagnosis.1The Tyr329Ser variant is common in Ashkenazi Jewish patients. APBD is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, in the spectrum of glycogen storage disease type IV, caused by biallelic pathogenicGBE1variants.1-4The clinical presentation is heterogeneous, but the core symptoms include progressive neurogenic bladder, gait dysfunction due to mixed upper and lower motor neuron involvement (ie, myeloneuropathy), and cognitive impairment at or after age 40 years.1-4Lower motor neuron involvement is due to a length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy and polyradiculopathies.1-4In severe cases, an Alzheimer disease–like dementia phenotype was previously reported.1-4The pace of progression is usually slow. In one of the largest series to date, the median age for onset of symptoms was 51 years and for wheelchair dependence and death was 63 and 70 years, respectively.4Radiographic findings may be nonspecific and include widespread confluent and symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter abnormalities in the periventricular regions, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and external capsule. Additional clues that (if present) suggest APBD include involvement of corticospinal tracts and medial lemniscus of the pons and medulla, superior cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei, and medullary and spinal cord atrophy.1-4Although nerve biopsy may show polyglucosan bodies, definitive diagnosis is established by genetic testing via targetedGBE1sequencing, multigene panels that includeGBE1, whole-exome sequencing or whole-genome sequencing.2,3Treatment is supportive and includes symptomatic management of spasticity, neurogenic bladder, dysautonomia, and cognitive decline.2,3 Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation is caused by autosomal recessive variants in theDARS2gene.5Typical presentation occurs in early childhood, but adult-onset disease has been described.5Core clinical features include slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-extremity predominant spasticity, and dorsal column dysfunction.5Axonal neuropathy can occur. MRI reveals a distinct T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the cerebral white matter sparing the U-fibers, involvement of posterior limbs of the internal capsule, splenium of the corpus callosum, trigeminal nerve tracts, cerebellum, and the dorsal column and lateral corticospinal tracts of the medulla and spinal cord.5Features that allow distinction from APBD are an earlier age of onset, prominent cerebellar and sensory ataxia, and characteristic spinal cord signal abnormalities.5 LMNB-1–related autosomal dominant leukodystrophy (ADLD) presents between ages 40 to 60 years with dysautonomia followed by corticospinal tract and cerebellar dysfunction, resulting in spastic ataxia and tremors.6MRI in ADLD can show T2/FLAIR hyperintensity predominantly in a frontoparietal distribution following the corticospinal tracts through the posterior limb of the internal capsule toward the medulla and upper and middle cerebellar peduncles.6,7Spinal cord atrophy is common and can be associated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the entire cord white matter.6,7Some distinguishing features from APBD are the different imaging pattern, sparing of the peripheral nervous system, and more prominent cerebellar dysfunction.6 Alexander disease is caused by autosomal dominantGFAPgene variants that can present across the lifespan, with adult onset occurring in approximately 33% of 1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

case_info.explanation: C. Adult polyglucosan body disease The presentation was suggestive of adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD), and a multigene panel revealed a compound heterozygous pathogenic missense variant in the glycogen branching enzyme 1 (GBE1) gene (c.986A>C (p.Tyr329Ser) and c.691 + 2T>C (IVS5 + 2T>C)), confirming this diagnosis.1The Tyr329Ser variant is common in Ashkenazi Jewish patients. APBD is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, in the spectrum of glycogen storage disease type IV, caused by biallelic pathogenicGBE1variants.1-4The clinical presentation is heterogeneous, but the core symptoms include progressive neurogenic bladder, gait dysfunction due to mixed upper and lower motor neuron involvement (ie, myeloneuropathy), and cognitive impairment at or after age 40 years.1-4Lower motor neuron involvement is due to a length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy and polyradiculopathies.1-4In severe cases, an Alzheimer disease–like dementia phenotype was previously reported.1-4The pace of progression is usually slow. In one of the largest series to date, the median age for onset of symptoms was 51 years and for wheelchair dependence and death was 63 and 70 years, respectively.4Radiographic findings may be nonspecific and include widespread confluent and symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter abnormalities in the periventricular regions, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and external capsule. Additional clues that (if present) suggest APBD include involvement of corticospinal tracts and medial lemniscus of the pons and medulla, superior cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei, and medullary and spinal cord atrophy.1-4Although nerve biopsy may show polyglucosan bodies, definitive diagnosis is established by genetic testing via targetedGBE1sequencing, multigene panels that includeGBE1, whole-exome sequencing or whole-genome sequencing.2,3Treatment is supportive and includes symptomatic management of spasticity, neurogenic bladder, dysautonomia, and cognitive decline.2,3 Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation is caused by autosomal recessive variants in theDARS2gene.5Typical presentation occurs in early childhood, but adult-onset disease has been described.5Core clinical features include slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-extremity predominant spasticity, and dorsal column dysfunction.5Axonal neuropathy can occur. MRI reveals a distinct T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the cerebral white matter sparing the U-fibers, involvement of posterior limbs of the internal capsule, splenium of the corpus callosum, trigeminal nerve tracts, cerebellum, and the dorsal column and lateral corticospinal tracts of the medulla and spinal cord.5Features that allow distinction from APBD are an earlier age of onset, prominent cerebellar and sensory ataxia, and characteristic spinal cord signal abnormalities.5 LMNB-1–related autosomal dominant leukodystrophy (ADLD) presents between ages 40 to 60 years with dysautonomia followed by corticospinal tract and cerebellar dysfunction, resulting in spastic ataxia and tremors.6MRI in ADLD can show T2/FLAIR hyperintensity predominantly in a frontoparietal distribution following the corticospinal tracts through the posterior limb of the internal capsule toward the medulla and upper and middle cerebellar peduncles.6,7Spinal cord atrophy is common and can be associated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the entire cord white matter.6,7Some distinguishing features from APBD are the different imaging pattern, sparing of the peripheral nervous system, and more prominent cerebellar dysfunction.6 Alexander disease is caused by autosomal dominantGFAPgene variants that can present across the lifespan, with adult onset occurring in approximately 33% of cases.8The typical adult phenotype includes bulbar symptoms (eg, palatal myoclonus, dysarthria, dysphagia), cerebellar dysfunction, and corticospinal tract involvement resulting in spastic weakness.8,9Other features include sleep disorder, dysautonomia, and parkinsonism.8A typical MRI finding is cervicomedullary atrophy with relative pontine sparing, known as thetadpole sign.8,9Other potential findings include cerebellar signal abnormalities, contrast-enhancing lesions, and periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities.8,9Distinguishing features from APBD include sparing of the peripheral nervous system and lack of the extensive supratentorial signal abnormalities and extensive spinal cord atrophy seen in this case.8,9

You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Case:
A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

case_info.explanation: C. Adult polyglucosan body disease The presentation was suggestive of adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD), and a multigene panel revealed a compound heterozygous pathogenic missense variant in the glycogen branching enzyme 1 (GBE1) gene (c.986A>C (p.Tyr329Ser) and c.691 + 2T>C (IVS5 + 2T>C)), confirming this diagnosis.1The Tyr329Ser variant is common in Ashkenazi Jewish patients. APBD is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, in the spectrum of glycogen storage disease type IV, caused by biallelic pathogenicGBE1variants.1-4The clinical presentation is heterogeneous, but the core symptoms include progressive neurogenic bladder, gait dysfunction due to mixed upper and lower motor neuron involvement (ie, myeloneuropathy), and cognitive impairment at or after age 40 years.1-4Lower motor neuron involvement is due to a length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy and polyradiculopathies.1-4In severe cases, an Alzheimer disease–like dementia phenotype was previously reported.1-4The pace of progression is usually slow. In one of the largest series to date, the median age for onset of symptoms was 51 years and for wheelchair dependence and death was 63 and 70 years, respectively.4Radiographic findings may be nonspecific and include widespread confluent and symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter abnormalities in the periventricular regions, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and external capsule. Additional clues that (if present) suggest APBD include involvement of corticospinal tracts and medial lemniscus of the pons and medulla, superior cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei, and medullary and spinal cord atrophy.1-4Although nerve biopsy may show polyglucosan bodies, definitive diagnosis is established by genetic testing via targetedGBE1sequencing, multigene panels that includeGBE1, whole-exome sequencing or whole-genome sequencing.2,3Treatment is supportive and includes symptomatic management of spasticity, neurogenic bladder, dysautonomia, and cognitive decline.2,3 Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation is caused by autosomal recessive variants in theDARS2gene.5Typical presentation occurs in early childhood, but adult-onset disease has been described.5Core clinical features include slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-extremity predominant spasticity, and dorsal column dysfunction.5Axonal neuropathy can occur. MRI reveals a distinct T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the cerebral white matter sparing the U-fibers, involvement of posterior limbs of the internal capsule, splenium of the corpus callosum, trigeminal nerve tracts, cerebellum, and the dorsal column and lateral corticospinal tracts of the medulla and spinal cord.5Features that allow distinction from APBD are an earlier age of onset, prominent cerebellar and sensory ataxia, and characteristic spinal cord signal abnormalities.5 LMNB-1–related autosomal dominant leukodystrophy (ADLD) presents between ages 40 to 60 years with dysautonomia followed by corticospinal tract and cerebellar dysfunction, resulting in spastic ataxia and tremors.6MRI in ADLD can show T2/FLAIR hyperintensity predominantly in a frontoparietal distribution following the corticospinal tracts through the posterior limb of the internal capsule toward the medulla and upper and middle cerebellar peduncles.6,7Spinal cord atrophy is common and can be associated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the entire cord white matter.6,7Some distinguishing features from APBD are the different imaging pattern, sparing of the peripheral nervous system, and more prominent cerebellar dysfunction.6 Alexander disease is caused by autosomal dominantGFAPgene variants that can present across the lifespan, with adult onset occurring in approximately 33% of cases.8The typical adult phenotype includes bulbar symptoms (eg, palatal myoclonus, dysarthria, dysphagia), cerebellar dysfunction, and corticospinal tract involvement resulting in spastic weakness.8,9Other features include sleep disorder, dysautonomia, and parkinsonism.8A typical MRI finding is cervicomedullary atrophy with relative pontine sparing, known as thetadpole sign.8,9Other potential findings include cerebellar signal abnormalities, contrast-enhancing lesions, and periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities.8,9Distinguishing features from APBD include sparing of the peripheral nervous system and lack of the extensive supratentorial signal abnormalities and extensive spinal cord atrophy seen in this case.8,9

A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

case_info.explanation: C. Adult polyglucosan body disease The presentation was suggestive of adult polyglucosan body disease (APBD), and a multigene panel revealed a compound heterozygous pathogenic missense variant in the glycogen branching enzyme 1 (GBE1) gene (c.986A>C (p.Tyr329Ser) and c.691 + 2T>C (IVS5 + 2T>C)), confirming this diagnosis.1The Tyr329Ser variant is common in Ashkenazi Jewish patients. APBD is a rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder, in the spectrum of glycogen storage disease type IV, caused by biallelic pathogenicGBE1variants.1-4The clinical presentation is heterogeneous, but the core symptoms include progressive neurogenic bladder, gait dysfunction due to mixed upper and lower motor neuron involvement (ie, myeloneuropathy), and cognitive impairment at or after age 40 years.1-4Lower motor neuron involvement is due to a length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy and polyradiculopathies.1-4In severe cases, an Alzheimer disease–like dementia phenotype was previously reported.1-4The pace of progression is usually slow. In one of the largest series to date, the median age for onset of symptoms was 51 years and for wheelchair dependence and death was 63 and 70 years, respectively.4Radiographic findings may be nonspecific and include widespread confluent and symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintense white matter abnormalities in the periventricular regions, posterior limb of the internal capsule, and external capsule. Additional clues that (if present) suggest APBD include involvement of corticospinal tracts and medial lemniscus of the pons and medulla, superior cerebellar peduncles and dentate nuclei, and medullary and spinal cord atrophy.1-4Although nerve biopsy may show polyglucosan bodies, definitive diagnosis is established by genetic testing via targetedGBE1sequencing, multigene panels that includeGBE1, whole-exome sequencing or whole-genome sequencing.2,3Treatment is supportive and includes symptomatic management of spasticity, neurogenic bladder, dysautonomia, and cognitive decline.2,3 Leukoencephalopathy with brainstem and spinal cord involvement and lactate elevation is caused by autosomal recessive variants in theDARS2gene.5Typical presentation occurs in early childhood, but adult-onset disease has been described.5Core clinical features include slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, lower-extremity predominant spasticity, and dorsal column dysfunction.5Axonal neuropathy can occur. MRI reveals a distinct T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the cerebral white matter sparing the U-fibers, involvement of posterior limbs of the internal capsule, splenium of the corpus callosum, trigeminal nerve tracts, cerebellum, and the dorsal column and lateral corticospinal tracts of the medulla and spinal cord.5Features that allow distinction from APBD are an earlier age of onset, prominent cerebellar and sensory ataxia, and characteristic spinal cord signal abnormalities.5 LMNB-1–related autosomal dominant leukodystrophy (ADLD) presents between ages 40 to 60 years with dysautonomia followed by corticospinal tract and cerebellar dysfunction, resulting in spastic ataxia and tremors.6MRI in ADLD can show T2/FLAIR hyperintensity predominantly in a frontoparietal distribution following the corticospinal tracts through the posterior limb of the internal capsule toward the medulla and upper and middle cerebellar peduncles.6,7Spinal cord atrophy is common and can be associated T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the entire cord white matter.6,7Some distinguishing features from APBD are the different imaging pattern, sparing of the peripheral nervous system, and more prominent cerebellar dysfunction.6 Alexander disease is caused by autosomal dominantGFAPgene variants that can present across the lifespan, with adult onset occurring in approximately 33% of cases.8The typical adult phenotype includes bulbar symptoms (eg, palatal myoclonus, dysarthria, dysphagia), cerebellar dysfunction, and corticospinal tract involvement resulting in spastic weakness.8,9Other features include sleep disorder, dysautonomia, and parkinsonism.8A typical MRI finding is cervicomedullary atrophy with relative pontine sparing, known as thetadpole sign.8,9Other potential findings include cerebellar signal abnormalities, contrast-enhancing lesions, and periventricular white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities.8,9Distinguishing features from APBD include sparing of the peripheral nervous system and lack of the extensive supratentorial signal abnormalities and extensive spinal cord atrophy seen in this case.8,9
